analysis:
Examined all seven batch analyses and verified their supported conclusions against the available source replay, including file metadata and patches. ClusterSetupLinkExchange.swift head 113–125 adds a public-value pairing identity; head 170–184 records the identity used by each responder without exposing edge secrets or changing key derivation. ClusterServiceControl.swift head 109–119 adopts shared listener-change detection and configured listener selection/policy; head 176–182 additionally invalidates control state after local member identity changes. These changes do not independently demonstrate weakened authentication or serving authorization.
The documentation at inference.md head 3541–3575 and changelog.d/cluster-service-follows-repair.md:3–6 describes periodic rebinding, pairing refresh, stopping after pairing removal, and retaining listeners on unreadable storage. Retention is not demonstrated to be a newly introduced revocation bypass; previously running listeners also retained their pairing. No supported new plaintext exposure, cache-scope weakening, billing change, attestation bypass, privileged-helper change or installer exposure follows from the supplied changes. Surrounding cache, cancellation and encrypted-stream descriptions are unchanged and do not establish regressions under T-008, T-010, T-041 or T-050.
Material integration uncertainty remains: the replay omits 15 reviewed source units, including the decisive ClusterService.swift listener lifecycle implementation. Review its head 164–175 and 337–420 with listenerChange/listenerSelection, Listening defaults, Responder.stop and command dispatch to verify cable-restricted policy, retirement of old connections/queued commands, and coherent setup/control authority after re-pairing or removal. Confirm fresh ceremony epochs justify excluding edge secrets from identity comparison. These contracts affect A-001/A-018 and authorization-freshness concerns analogous to T-053; cluster pairing must not be mistaken for coordinator serving permission. Missing implementations limit this conclusion rather than proving either safety or a vulnerability.
